text: Quick notes on the pronunciation of Rafa Câmara’s name emoji:post-misc: Misc With Rafa now in F1, I foresee a return of the Barrikkello/Barritchello confusion of old when people hear him/other Brazilians pronounce his name, so here’s a quick explanation (FWIW, it’s Ba-hee-kke-llo in Pt-Br) Firstly, an “R” at the beginning of a word in Brazilian Portuguese has an aspirated “H” sound. So it’s not Wraffa, it’s Haffa. Think of the word “huff” Now for his last name. Most english-speakers will pronounce it as kah-MAH-rah, like a Chevy Camaro with an “A” at the end. And that would be 100% correct if it were Camara, but it’s actually Câmara, with a circumflex accent (the hat thing) on the first A That changes it to a lower sound. It sounds like the first part of the word “come” (just the k-sound, ignore the m-) It also makes the first syllable the tonic, so it becomes KUH-muh-ruh Note that the other syllables also changed from a (more open) to u (closed) because the tonic was pulled to the first one And if you wanted to be really precise, the last syllable is a rolled r, so rrrruh, not wruh, but that’s probably too specific Finally, do note this is all just for curiosity’s sake. No Brazilian is ever going to be mad if someone says Wraffa KaMAHrah. As a people we’re very casual about this sort of thing and we know many of the sounds in Portuguese are very unintuitive for non-speakers Cheers!

text: (Un)popular Opinion: Excessively good reliability makes the sport much worse The most obvious reasoning is that it makes it less fun to watch, as random reliability issues would always add a feeling of uncertainty, which is what sports are all about for me. One reason football is the most watched sport in the world, beyond its ease to understand at a basic level, is that there's so much unpredictability to it. Upsets happen so so often. However F1 is also an engineering sport, and thus in my opinion any time a technical aspect reaches a point whereby everyone is near perfect, you have to artificially bring in new challenges to keep it interesting. Very much hope that the next reg set does this with the engine changes, but even then there are so few constructors that it's still expected to be pretty stable. The only real argument I can think of for being pro-perfect-reliability is safety concerns, which I agree with wholeheartedly but you can have bad reliability without risking the drivers lives in my opinion. How do others feel about this, is this a common feeling or just me?

text: [Luke Smith] In the first two runs of his test, Rafael Câmara had improved by seven-tenths. “Because that second run, 18.5, was so good, I thought maybe he could improve a tenth or half a tenth," Komatsu recalled. “Do you know how much he improved by? Four-and-a-half tenths.” Ayao Komatsu could not believe what he was seeing. The live data coming from the Haas Formula 1 car as it lapped the Portimāo circuit in southern Portugal suggested that it was going to crash. But Rafael Câmara had everything under control. “He was braking really late. I was like, ‘No way he’s going to make it stick,’” Komatsu recalled in an interview with The Athletic . “You could see it on the speed trace (car telemetry data). But bang, he hits the apex, and he’s out of the corner. It was sensational.” Komatsu’s eyes then turned to the stopwatch as Câmara neared the finish line. In the first two runs of his private F1 test with Haas, his shot at securing an F1 seat for 2027, he’d already improved by seven-tenths of a second, from 1:19.2 to 1:18.5. The pole position lap time for the most recent Portuguese Grand Prix at the track — in 2021 — was a 1:18.3. But with the track growing hotter and the wind picking up, Komatsu doubted he’d be able to go faster. “Because that second run, 18.5, was so good, I thought maybe he could improve a tenth or half a tenth, or maybe he goes slower by overdriving. “Do you know how much he improved by? Four-and-a-half tenths.” A 1m18.05. At that moment, Komatsu knew he had to sign Câmara to race Haas for 2027.

text: My Attempt at visualising the Rwanda F1 Circuit. On 13 October 2026, Formula 1 announced a 10-year deal to race in Rwanda, with the first race planned for the early 2030s. That announcement came with a preview of what the circuit could look like. One single Image. Using that single preview image as my reference, I’ve spent the last 24 or so hours making a “best guess” version for Assetto Corsa! It measures 4.65 km , with approximately 70 metres between the highest and lowest points of the racing line. There are some massive climbs and drops! The first challenge was working out where it belonged. Matching the airport visible in the background to satellite imagery gave me a starting point, then perspective alignment helped translate the angled render into a layout I could build. The surrounding landscape uses satellite imagery and elevation data, extending out towards the distant hills. From there, I’ve built up the circuit and its surroundings: the colourful striped run-off areas, yellow-and-white kerbs, lakeside sections, barriers, service roads and bridges. The distinctive grandstands with their joined funnel-shaped roofs were modelled from the preview, alongside pit garages, There’s no proper pit building in place, as I really couldn’t make it out from the one angle we have.

text: Making a vintage F1 simulation for PC and Mac OS I got into game dev this year after my old career as a filmmaker ended and having been watching F1 since 1994 I thought I'd stick to what I know. Here it is, GP2 Revival - a new simulation engine with an advanced physics engine, dynamic weather simulation, and a custom 3D engine, that started life based on a recompile of the original Grand Prix 2 game from 1996 earlier this year. The original was a cult classic game, by the legendary Geoff Crammond. In those days there were only 3 racing sims at the cutting edge of the market - Grand Prix 2, Indycars and Grand Prix Legends, which later went on to become iRacing, Max's favourite past time. Each is a work of art in it's own right. Mine, GP2 Revival is a hybrid - My custom3D engine breathes new life into GP2 making use of modern hardware but keeping the charm of the original cars and tracks from the 1994 season. The finished game will have 4K / 120fps, sim racing wheel and force feedback support, and you can even import Grand Prix 4 mod packs so you can bring in a range of seasons into the game between the 80s and the modern era. I'm aiming to get VR working by Christmas and wet weather simulation, which the original never got! I've got a dev blog about it here https://gp2rev.com and check out the Patreon https://www.patreon.com/gp2revival for updates on my progress (hope it is ok to post this here mods). Would love to hear the feedback of real F1 fans.

text: Mercedes completed 125 Laps in Pirelli’s 2027 Intermediate Tyre Test Real rain also played its part in helping complete the day of testing organised by Pirelli at Magny-Cours as part of the development programme for next season’s wet-weather tyres. Mercedes reserve driver Frederik Vesti evaluated a number of Intermediate tyre solutions today, featuring different compounds and constructions, with the aim of identifying the prototypes capable of delivering the best warm-up performance. The track remained wet throughout the morning thanks to overnight rainfall. In the afternoon, the level of surface moisture was maintained using the circuit’s artificial watering system. Vesti completed a total of 125 laps, covering 551 kilometres, with a best time of 1:30.284. Track temperature peaked at 22°C, while the air temperature reached 20°C. The test programme will continue tomorrow with the evaluation of dry-weather compounds, also with a view to defining the crossover window more precisely. Should rainfall continue overnight or during the day, the focus of the work could once again switch to wet-weather tyres.

text: [16-18 October] No Formula 1? No problem! Check out the other racing series that hit the track this weekend. We are slap bang in the middle of two Formula 1 triple headers, so there's definitely no lack of four-wheeled entertainment. If you're still looking for a substitute drug for the upcoming F1-less weekend, I've gathered your main candidates in this list. The intended season opener in Qatar was first postponed and recently replaced entirely , as was the season finale in Bahrain. The season will now culminate in Monza instead, preceded by this weekend's 6 Hours of Barcelona which will be WEC's first non-testing visit to Catalunya. The four-time F1 world champion joins a stacked 61-car grid that will be vying for both victory in the three-hour race and glory in the unsettled title fights. Due to this shift, the Autopolis race won't be run with half-ballast but the usual 2 kg per amassed point. text: Form after the triple-header: who is actually fastest right now (race pace, every 2026 round) I keep a form model for the 2026 season and after Baku–Sepang–Singapore the picture has changed enough to be worth a post. Chart attached; the interactive version with every driver and round is at f1-strategy.com/form . How it is measured. For every race I take the clean green-flag laps (no in/out laps, no neutralised laps, nothing over 107 % of the driver’s median), fuel-correct them at 0.035 s per lap, and compute each car’s pace as a gap to the fastest car in the race, in per cent of lap time. That is the dot on the chart. “Form” is then an exponentially weighted average over the season with a half-life of three races – the latest race counts most, but one race cannot flip it. “Trend” is the mean of the last five races against the five before. Same method for qualifying, using the best lap against pole. Teams, race pace (form / trend): Mercedes 0.16 / −0.04 Red Bull 0.29 / −0.64 Ferrari 0.33 / +0.12 McLaren 0.34 / −0.09 Mercedes is still the best car over the season, and that is not a sentimental weighting – they were fastest or within 0.01 % in nine of seventeen races. But the dots for the last three read 0.00, 0.17, 0.29: Baku fastest, then slower than Red Bull at Sepang and slower than three teams in Singapore. The team spent the Singapore weekend A/B-testing a new front wing (Russell old, Antonelli new) and says the new one was the faster car by Sunday. Whether that is a one-off or the start of a slide is exactly what the model cannot tell yet; the half-life is the honest answer. Red Bull is the story. From R1 to R12 their race pace sat between 0.4 and 1.6 % off – the worst of the big four in eight of them. Then 0.37 at Monza, 0.23 Madrid, 0.09 Baku, 0.00 Sepang, 0.02 Singapore. The form line is still at 0.29 because the half-life drags Zandvoort along; the dots say they have been the fastest or second-fastest race car for three rounds. Two wins from pole in two weeks is what that looks like. The trend, −0.64, is the steepest improvement of any team by a factor of two. Ferrari is the one where the headline number lies. Trend +0.12 says they are fading; the last three dots read 0.53, 0.29, 0.00. The fastest race car in Singapore, by our clean-lap measure, was the Ferrari – Leclerc’s second stint on new softs after the VSC was the quickest sustained pace of the race. The trend is Monza (1.03) sitting in the five-race window. Give it two races and it flips. What is real: Ferrari qualifies at Red Bull’s level (0.05 s off pole in Singapore) and has been losing the start, not the race. McLaren was the fastest race car in Spa, Hungary and Madrid and has not been better than 0.2 % off since. Norris’s own verdict after Singapore – “clearly the fourth fastest at the moment” – matches the dots (0.70, 0.27, 0.20). The car is not slow; the other three found something in September and McLaren did not. Drivers, race pace form: Verstappen 0.24, Antonelli 0.28, Leclerc 0.30, then a step to Norris 0.54, Piastri 0.54, Russell 0.56, Hamilton 0.59. The gap between the top three and the rest is new; in August it did not exist. Verstappen’s trend (−0.52) is partly the car, but Hadjar in the same car trends −0.60 from a much higher base (0.85), which is the usual pattern when a car comes good: the second driver gains more. Antonelli’s +0.10 is three races of 0.71, 0.17, 0.29 – not a crisis, but the championship leader is no longer in the fastest car. Hamilton’s +0.24 is the weakest trend in the top seven, and Singapore (0.54 against Leclerc’s 0.00 in the same car) is the largest intra-team race-pace gap at Ferrari this year; the medium first stint and the 44-lap soft explain most of it, which is strategy, not pace. Russell’s 1.43 in Singapore is traffic from P19 and should be read as noise. Caveats. Race-pace gaps are measured on clean laps only, so a car that spends the race in traffic (Russell, Hadjar) is under-measured; a car that runs alone at the front is measured at its managed pace, not its limit. Sprint weekends have one practice session and the race itself is the only long-run data. And a half-life of three races is a choice: shorter and the chart jumps with every Safety Car, longer and it misses Red Bull’s September. The interactive page lets you see each round on its own. What it means for Austin. Four cars within 0.3 % of each other in Singapore race pace, two of them within 0.02, and a championship leader whose car was fourth-fastest on Sunday with 150 points left and a 102-point lead. The title is not in doubt; the last six races are. Corrections and alternative weightings welcome – the method is the same as in the briefings and aftermaths posted here before.

text: [OC] I built F1 Almanac - An interactive archive of teammate H2Hs, driver connection webs, race visualiser and more Hey r/formula1 , I want to share a passion project I’ve been working on: F1 Almanac . Like many of you, I spend way too much time debating driver matchups and hunting down data to back up my takes. I built F1 Almanac to be an all-in-one interactive hub that replaces the endless tab-shuffling between Wikipedia tables, fragmented timing sheets, and scattered databases. Here is what you can explore: Teammate H2H (Qualifying & Race) : Pick any team and season to see the complete breakdown of raw time deltas, percentage pace gaps, finishing distributions, and sprint comparisons between any two teammates. See more info here . Driver vs. Driver Comparisons (Qualifying & Race) : Compare any two drivers from a season, even if they drove for different teams. Post-Race Debriefs : Deep dive into recent Grands Prix with tyre strategy stints, degradation curves, and lap-by-lap pace progression. Driver & Team Profiles : Complete historical career timelines, stats and records of your favourite drivers and teams. Season Stats & Standings : Historical season progression charts and results matrices. Interactive Teammate Web : The ultimate "Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon" for F1. Explore driver connections and teammate history across the entire history of Formula 1. See more info here . 2D Race Visualiser : Relive races through an interactive replay scrubber showing relative track positions and intervals throughout the race (available for races from 2023 onwards, with Circle of Doom views back to 1996). text: Why is everyone so focused on ICE performance when the MGU-K could be just as big a differentiator? It seems like everyone is always focusing on the ICE power of the different manufacturers, ie Redbull having the strongest ICE or whatever. But it would seem to me like the electric motor, inverter, motor control algorithm, etc would be equally if not more critical, since the electric power is the overwhelming limitation. If one manufacturer had a 3% average efficiency advantage across the range for example, with the 50/50 power split that would be huge. Also as an engineer I know very well that all technology can be improved, but my sense is that the ICE space has long ago been optimized to a very high level using tech that is common knowledge across teams, whereas there is still a ton of rapid development and advancements being made in the electric motor design space (see YASA for example, coincidentally owned by Merc). For the record my field of expertise is electric motor/inverter design so it's on my mind more than the average f1 viewer....

text: Serious debate: Is the tire the most important and irreplaceable technology in automotive history Hi everyone. I’ve been thinking about this and wanted to open up a debate. Nowadays, everyone gets blinded by horsepower, electric motors, autonomous driving, or massive dashboard screens. But if we analyze it with pure logic and physics, isn't the tire the single greatest automotive technology ever? You can have 1,000 HP or the most advanced AI, but if those four patches of rubber—each the size of a palm—fail or lose grip, the car is useless. Even if we imagine a future with low-altitude hovering cars, the main issue will always be the lack of friction to brake in an emergency at 70 mph. Physics forces us back to the ground. I feel like we live with a "traction blindness" where nobody values tires, and people only care about going faster or looking prettier. Why does the general public ignore tires so much when they structurally sustain absolutely everything? What do you think? Am I right, or am I overthinking it?

text: F1 announces new African Grand Prix held in Rwanda from ‘early 2030s’ Formula 1 has announced it will return to Africa for the first time in nearly 40 years after signing a deal with Rwanda to host a race by the early 2030s. A new track constructed in Bugesera on the outskirts of Rwanda’s capital, Kigali, will stage the new race that will be known as the African Grand Prix presented by Visit Rwanda after signing a 10-year deal. No year has been determined for the first staging of the event, with F1 saying it will join the calendar in the “early 2030s”. Should that be as soon as 2030, it would mark 37 years since F1 last raced in Africa, when Kyalami in South Africa hosted its final grand prix in 1993. Since then, the sport has expanded its calendar rapidly across Asia and North America, making Africa the only continent that does not feature on its schedule.

text: Hot take: RBR are deciding between Lindblad and Tsolov, not Lawson and Tsolov I genuinely think Liam Lawson’s seat at Racing Bulls is already secured for 2027, and the decision RBR are actually wrestling with is whether to retain Arvid Lindblad or promote Nikola Tsolov. Liam has experience across both Red Bull teams, has shown he can handle the pressure of the Red Bull system, and provides a useful benchmark for whichever young driver they want to develop next. Arvid has shown flashes of serious potential, but he’s also had some rough patches. Meanwhile, Tsolov is making a case for promotion, and Red Bull will need to decide whether another year of development would benefit Arvid or whether it’s time to give Tsolov his opportunity. If they’re serious about developing their next generation of drivers, having Lawson as the experienced constant makes sense. My suspicion is that Liam already knows he’s staying, while Arvid’s future is still being decided. Pure speculation, obviously, but I do think the real fight for that second Racing Bulls seat is Lindblad vs Tsolov. What do y’all think?

text: Ferrari Pitwall Communication Singapore was a very frustrating watch as a Ferrari fan (and a very boring watch as an F1 fan). I don't think Ferrari really messed up Hamilton's strategy all that badly - pitting him that early was probably not ideal and then staying out was Hamilton's call, not the teams' call, so it's live-by-the-sword-die-by-the-sword. However. The communication between Hamilton and his race engineer is atrocious. When he asks them 'what was the pace of the other cars at the end of their stints on the soft tires' it felt like they were getting out the dictionary to translate it - they had absolutely no clue what he was asking. In general there is absolutely zero rapport between Hamilton and Carlo Santi - when Hamilton said 'I want to stay out' Santi should have said "Absolutely not, trust me on this" but somehow I can't imagine Santi ever saying those words. It feels like if he was asked to say that sentence in a job interview he would just quit on spot - it doesn't feel like he's capable of being that direct. Similarly, there was the issue of Hamilton pitting early and then getting stuck behind LeClerc on faster tires. If he was on a different strategy then it's a no-brainer - tell him to move out of the way! Ferrari has done this before. But somehow they get themselves into knots trying to figure out how to communicate something simple to their drivers that probably was - or definitely should have been - discussed before the race. And if they said before the race they're not doing it then tell him "No, we discussed this". If this was Mercedes Toto would come on the radio and say 'Lewis this is Toto, please let Charles by, he's on a different strategy'. I'm not saying Ferrari needs to copy Mercedes but someone on the pitwall needs to be the adult in the room. I literally cannot see how Ferrari can win a championship without an enormous car advantage if they can't sort this out. It's so frustrating to watch. How is this not obvious to the management at Ferrari?
